items.title: Benny Waters interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 1, 1995
items.q: But when he had Benny Carter in the band and he also got the great Louis Armstrong. And when he got the great Louis Armstrong, that, they did just like Ella Fitzgerald did with Chick Webb, you know, lifted them right on up higher and higher, you know?

ctx.x: Yeah. Ninety years, wow. Have you have occasion during your many years of experience, to work with either Count Basie or Joe Williams?

No I haven’t. No I haven’t. I wish I did. But I tell you I did work with a band that, well I may be saying something that people will agree, you know, but I had a pleasure working with Jimmie Lunceford and I thought it was a greater band than Count Basie. Not musically. Not musically. Exclusive musically. But for all around entertaining and music combined, I think it was a better band than Count Basie. So I had the pleasure of working with Jimmie a couple of years, I mean Jimmie Lunceford see. And I worked with…
Oh that’s marvelous. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

items.title: 68002_Benny Waters oral history interview
items.q: I wasn't copying Sidney Bechet because I didn't hear much of, that much of those, that period

ctx.x: most of the time we faked it, things like that. And the riffs that we were playing is similar to the things that you hearing today. [ ], three-part harmony - alto, trombone and trumpet. So he was just (sings), you know, one of those kind of things. And the, we could do that very fast, we could do it real easy because everybody had big ears, you know, they could hear, see. And I could fake it and Driver could fake it and the trumpet player could fake, and we had the right harmonies.

Some of the first solos, conceived, improvised jazz solos that we recognize as such now, that we can learn about - those of us who weren't there then - through records, seem to indicate to us that the people who were really doin' it, maybe the only ones who were doin' it at first, were Sidney Bechet and Louis Armstrong on the disc. 'Course it was King Oliver, at least for that matter there was Frankie Trumbauer, Johnny Dodds. When you say they were taking jazz solos as we would recognize them today as jazz solos…
